steps.say: Choledochal cysts come in five shapes that dictate five different operations. The commonest is a fusiform swelling of the main bile duct outside the liver. Then come pouch diverticula, the small choledochocele at the papilla, intrahepatic Caroli disease, and combined patterns. Naming the type correctly is the whole ball game.
steps.tx: **Todani** types I to V (five-shape classification of bile duct cysts) span fusiform extrahepatic dilation, saccular diverticulum, choledochocele, intrahepatic **Caroli disease** (segmental intrahepatic duct sacculations) and combined disease, with type I commonest by far. Correct classification decides between radical excision and endoscopic therapy.

steps.say: These cysts are born from a plumbing error where bile and pancreatic juice share too long a common pipe. Pancreatic enzymes are washed back into the bile duct because the junction sits more than fifteen millimetres outside the wall. Years of chemical injury are ballooning the duct and, worse, seeding cancers even without a single stone.
steps.tx: Anomalous **pancreaticobiliary maljunction** (bile and pancreatic ducts joining outside the wall) with a long **common channel** (shared segment) past **15** mm, so pancreatic juice washes back into bile and grows the cyst toward gallbladder cancer. Reflux injury explains malignancy arising without any stones.

steps.say: Leaving any cyst wall behind is leaving a future cancer, so the whole extrahepatic duct comes out. The bile flow is rebuilt with a Roux loop of jejunum sewn to the hilum. That operation suits types one and four, because a retained stump carries up to a thirty percent lifetime cancer risk. The pancreatic end is cored out to leave nothing behind.
steps.tx: Complete **cyst excision** (removing the whole dilated extrahepatic duct) joined by a Roux loop to the hilum stays the choice for types I and IV, since a left-behind stump keeps up to **30** percent lifetime **cholangiocarcinoma risk** (bile duct cancer from the remnant). Pancreatic-end mucosectomy leaves no epithelium behind.

nodes.label: Types I and IV cyst confirmed

steps.say: Not every Todani type needs the big excision. The small type three bulge at the papilla is opened endoscopically with a simple sphincterotomy. Caroli disease limited to one lobe is cured by removing that lobe, while disease scattered through both lobes leaves transplantation as the only escape. Old drainage operations are abandoned because they preserve cancer risk.
steps.tx: Type **III** **choledochocele** (cystic papilla bulging into the duodenum) gets endoscopic **sphincterotomy** (cutting the papilla sphincter) rather than excision, while **Caroli disease** (intrahepatic sacculations with stone-filled ducts) limited to a single lobe is cured by removing that lobe, and scattered bilateral disease leaves transplantation as the escape. Drainage alone preserves cancer risk.

steps.say: Textbooks love the classic triad of pain, yellow eyes and a feelable lump, but real children rarely read the textbook. Fewer than one in five are showing all three together. Most arrive with pancreatitis attacks or ascending cholangitis instead. Antenatal scans now spot many cysts before birth, which changes counselling entirely.
steps.tx: Children usually arrive without the textbook picture: the trio of pain, yellow eyes and a **palpable mass** (feelable abdominal lump) behind the **classic triad** (three-sign picture) shows in under **20** percent, while pancreatitis or cholangitis brings most children in. Scans before birth increasingly find cysts antenatally.

steps.say: One adult cyst in ten already hides a cancer at the time of surgery, so the operation starts with detective work. Contrast is run through the ducts on the table and every thickened patch is biopsied. Frozen section gives the answer within minutes. Only a benign report lets the surgeon proceed to the planned reconstruction.
steps.tx: Intraoperative cholangiogram and biopsy of suspicious areas detect **synchronous cancer** (second malignancy present at operation) in **10** percent of adult cysts, mandating **frozen section** (rapid on-table pathology) before reconstruction. Thickened walls and nodules are sampled, and cancer converts the plan to radical resection.

vis.alt: Operative cholangiogram showing a dilated common bile duct with a filling defect.
vis.caption: On-table cholangiogram maps the cyst and spots synchronous lesions. Credit: Rebekah M. Padilla, Paul C. Hulsberg, Erik Soule, Taylor S. Harmo, Erik Eadie, Preston Ho.

steps.say: The job is not finished when the wound heals, because the join and any duct remnant need watching forever. Liver bloods and MRCP every year are catching strictures at the join and cancers in leftover pancreatic duct tissue. Stones forming above a tight join announce themselves with cholangitis. Lifelong follow up is the price of the original maljunction.
steps.tx: After the reconstruction, yearly liver tests plus MRCP hunt for **anastomotic stricture** (narrowing at the new join) and cancer in leftover pancreatic-duct tissue, and this **lifelong surveillance** (annual imaging without end) never stops. Stones gathering above tight joins announce themselves with repeat cholangitis.

steps.say: A gallbladder sitting on an anomalous junction is living dangerously even when scans show no stones and no cyst. cancers arise from reflux injury alone, so waiting for stones misses the point. Preventive removal is advised once the long common channel is proven.
steps.tx: Gallbladder cancer coexists with **maljunction** (anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction) even where no stones ever form, so **prophylactic cholecystectomy** (preventive gallbladder removal) is advised whenever the junction proves anomalous, cyst or not. Reflux injury explains the danger, so the gallbladder is removed with the cyst at the same operation.
